storm.summary_layperson: Thunderstorms tracking in from the west should reach the cove by around 6 PM, and unusually strong upper-level winds mean the sea breeze may actually help these storms stay organized rather than weaken them the way the cove's storms normally do, so expect similar or slightly stronger activity here than nearby inland areas until the sea breeze fades near sunset.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sea breeze convergence (8.1°F land-sea contrast, SSW flow) meeting an unusually strong 38-kt shear sets up a punch-through/intensification risk instead of the cove's usual protective choke — that boost fades as the sea breeze itself dies near 7:29 PM.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows a broken line of showers and storms 19–31 mi to the W/WSW/WNW, peaking at 54 dBZ within the scan. It's organized enough that this afternoon's Area Forecast Discussion mentions a Severe Thunderstorm Watch in effect until 9 PM — but that watch is described as covering "primarily western portions" of the forecast area, including the NYC metro and Nassau County, and the point-specific alert feed for Riverside/Greenwich shows nothing active here right now.

Normally the cove's cool Sound water throttles incoming storms, but tonight's setup works against that. CAPE is a moderate 900 J/kg — well under the level that punches through on instability alone — but 0–6 km shear is a notable 38 kt, and the AFD specifically calls out higher shear than recent similar setups, meaning better storm organization. At the same time the sea breeze is active (SSW flow, 8.1°F land-sea contrast). Sea breeze plus strong shear is the one combination the cove's usual marine-layer defense doesn't help with — instead of choking convection at the convergence boundary, it can help sustain or intensify it.

The water-air gap (8.1°F now) is real, and on a different night it would support the cove's usual "wind but less rain" story. But the pipeline didn't flag it as active protection for this event, and the arrival engine shows the nearest cell reaching the cove too soon (~5:54 PM) for any marine-layer buffer to apply anyway. The layer is also fading on its own — the 8°F gap now narrows to about 2°F by 7 PM as the air cools, dropping below the useful threshold around 6:29 PM.

The closest tracked cell (currently ~20 mi W, 38 dBZ core, closing at ~27 kt) is projected to reach the cove around 5:54 PM, window 5:44–6:04 PM, high confidence since the motion is radar-measured rather than modeled. A few more cells in the 22–25 mi range — one with a hotter 48 dBZ core — follow close behind, arriving roughly 5:58–6:13 PM.

Net call: expect the cove to see storm activity closer to full strength than its usual discount, through roughly sunset. Once the sea breeze fades near 7:29 PM the amplifying convergence effect goes with it, so any later-arriving activity (unlikely given current system motion) would face a more neutral setup. What would flip this call: if cloud cover or an early collapse kills the sea breeze before the cells arrive, the amplifying mechanism disappears; if CAPE keeps building toward the 1840 J/kg the model shows one hour out, that independently supports stronger updrafts regardless of the sea breeze.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 20 mi W closing at 27 kt, arriving too soon for the marine layer to help — and with the sea-breeze/shear combo favoring intensification rather than choking, expect it close to full strength.

wind.tactics_blurb: Sea breeze reinforced by a weak background southwesterly holds through early evening, but an approaching line of thunderstorms is likely to override the thermal around 6 PM — expect a sharp, brief gusty shift during passage, then a lighter post-storm westerly for the rest of the window. Start mid-line, favor open water away from the CT shore once the wind swings west.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This opens as a sea breeze reinforced by the background (gradient) wind: the 8.1°F gap between inland air (82.4°F) and Long Island Sound water is well above the 5°F thermal threshold, and the background gradient is a weak onshore southwesterly (~6 kt per the NWS forecast) — onshore and light enough to reinforce rather than fight the thermal. RYC is reading S/SSW 3.7 kt gusting 5.1, 10-min avg 2.7 kt; the western-LIS station cluster confirms it at a median SSW 195°, 5.0 kt.

HRRR's own surface forecast is badly out of step with what's actually happening: it's forecasting E 92° for this hour while stations are already at SSW 195° — a 103° divergence. The standard sea-breeze maturation correction only nudges that to ESE 107°, nowhere close to the observed direction, so for the current hour trust the stations, not the model.

That correction is largely moot anyway: the same storm complex tracked on radar (nearest cell 20 mi W, closing at 27 kt, ETA ~5:54 PM) is projected to cross the course in the middle of this window. Rather than a normal gradual sunset collapse, HRRR's hour-by-hour output shows the wind swinging to W/WSW behind the system — 276° down to 263° through the 7–10 PM hours — while 2m temperature drops from 82°F to 74°F as the outflow's cool pool settles in. That's a convective wind shift, not the smooth thermal evolution the regime framework normally describes, so treat the ESE 107° sea-breeze forecast as overtaken by events once the storm arrives.

Before the storm, pressure should be fairly even across the cove on this SSW flow — no strong side bias. During the ~6 PM passage, expect a short, sharp, highly gusty direction swing as the gust front crosses; given nearby cells carry 38–48 dBZ cores with 900–1840 J/kg of instability and 38 kt of shear, gusts well above the sustained model wind are plausible even though the hour's forecast sustained speed looks light. After passage, the channeled W/WSW flow typically holes up near the CT shore and runs stronger mid-Sound — favor the middle of the course, off the Belle Haven/Field Point shoreline.

Practically: a building 6-kt sea breeze at the start is fine dinghy racing, but the storm passage around 6 PM is a hard stop, not a shift to play — get off the water for that hour. Racing can resume after in a light 4–6 kt post-storm westerly, drifter-class for the rest of the window.
